name: Brow growth serum
lead: Brow growth serums are topical cosmetic products marketed to make eyebrows look thicker, fuller or longer. People apply them to sparse, over-plucked or naturally light brows in the hope of filling gaps and giving the face a more defined frame, as an alternative or complement to brow pencils, powders, microblading or transplants.[1][5] Many are peptide- or botanical-based; Wikipedia notes that some lash-growth brands use peptides rather than prostaglandins because of regulations in Canada and California.[1]

Brows matter for appearance because they shape expression and frame the eyes. Wikipedia describes eyebrows as short terminal hairs above each eye whose human functions include keeping sweat and debris out of the eye and communicating emotion, and notes that brow fashions have swung between full, thin and absent brows across eras.[5] Cosmetic serums sit alongside makeup tools such as pencils, gels and powders, cosmetic tattooing (microblading) and brow transplants as ways to change brow density.[5]

Published evidence on non-prescription brow serums is limited. A manufacturer-sponsored 2024 study tested a lash and brow serum for skin tolerability rather than for growth,[2] and a small registered trial of a brow serum is listed as completed, with no results located.[3]

chain: Apply a conditioning or peptide serum to the brow line
Claimed: hairs look longer or denser or break less
angle.text: People use the serums to try to thicken or lengthen brow hairs, particularly after over-plucking or when brows are naturally sparse. Makers describe peptides and botanicals as supporting the hairs, while some prescription lash products and one case report involve a prostaglandin drug.

infobox: Cosmetic claims; prostaglandin products restricted in some jurisdictions

paras: Cosmetic lash and brow conditioners using seed extracts, minerals and peptides have grown in popularity over the past decade.[1] They are distinct from prostaglandin-analog products: bimatoprost (Latisse) was introduced in 2009 as the first FDA-approved eyelash growth treatment, with noticeable growth over about 16 weeks.[1] Bimatoprost was originally approved in the US in 2001 under the brand name Lumigan to lower eye pressure in glaucoma.[4]
Brow serums are sold as liquids or gels applied with a brush to the brow line. Formulas typically list peptides, biotin, plant extracts or conditioning oils among their ingredients.

Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog. Wikipedia states that the US FDA approval for the eyelash use is for cosmetic purposes and describes its most common side effect as eye redness, affecting more than 10 percent of patients, with eyelid or periocular skin darkening and, rarely, permanent iris darkening also reported.[4] A published case report described a 60-year-old woman who applied a 0.03 percent solution daily for eight months and developed increased hair growth and thickening of the eyebrow hairs, which is a single case rather than a controlled trial.[4]

Because prostaglandin-based products are drugs where regulated, cosmetic serums that advertise peptides instead are the ones commonly sold without a prescription in markets such as Canada and California.[1]

Wikipedia lists tweezing, waxing, threading and trimming as grooming methods for brows, and makeup tools such as brushes, pencils, gels and powders for defining brows or filling sparse areas. Microblading, also called cosmetic tattooing, implants pigment in small cuts that mimic hair, and eyebrow transplants move follicles, usually from the back of the scalp, into brow areas lacking hair; people who have over-tweezed are described as common candidates.[5]

Cosmetics applied near the eye can cause skin sensitivity reactions, and manufacturers test products with irritation and patch tests. In a 2024 study sponsored by Bausch + Lomb, a lash and brow serum, an eye cream and a makeup remover from one brand were assessed in cumulative irritation and repeated insult patch test studies.[2] The study measured tolerability rather than hair growth.

Evidence specific to non-prescription brow serums is very limited. The 2024 sponsored study above evaluated safety and tolerability of one brand's lash and brow serum, not growth.[2] A trial registered as NCT07819721, 'Effects of CosmeRNA Brow Revitalizing Serum on Eyebrow Density and Length', enrolled 26 participants, started in April 2026 and is listed as completed; no results were found.[3] The only brow growth data for a drug in the sources is the single bimatoprost case report.[4]

card.summary: Cosmetic serums sold to thicken brows; published evidence is limited to a safety test and one small unreported trial.
card.note: Prostaglandin-containing products are drugs and regulated differently; growth data for cosmetic serums are lacking.

quick.overview:
Brow growth serums are topical cosmetics, often with peptides or plant extracts, marketed to make eyebrows look fuller. They are separate from prescription prostaglandin products such as bimatoprost.

Only limited research exists: one sponsored safety study of a lash and brow serum and one small registered trial without located results.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic serums generally claim to condition hair or support growth through peptides and botanicals; no published study confirms a mechanism for brow growth.
quick.risks: Products near the eye can cause irritation or allergic reactions, which manufacturers screen with patch tests. Prostaglandin-based products have additional documented effects such as eye redness and skin darkening.
